keyConcepts: 🔍 How to Do It Look for the setting: Where does the story take place? What details describe the place? Notice the characters: Who appears first? What do you learn about them from what they say and do? Find the first problem: What trouble or worry does the main character face? What makes it urgent? 🧠 Think about this As you read today, watch for the setting , the main character , and the first problem . Where does the family live? Who is Mrs. Frisby? What is the trouble? 💭 Think about this as you read today — you don't need to write anything here.

📌 Examples unwrap = un- + wrap | helper = help + -er | unhelpful = un- + help + -ful | resting = rest + -ing 🧩 Each word is missing one part. Type the missing base word or suffix . un — to take the cover off help — someone who helps rest — taking a break right now kind — in a kind way Check My Work 🌱 All correct!
📌 Let's try it together: "delirious"
Group A rab ·bit · gar ·den · win ·ter · pic ·nic Group B ba ·by · ti ·ger · o ·pen · mu ·sic

💎 What is courage? Courage means choosing to act even when you are afraid. 🐭 The book's courage moment: Mrs. Frisby is a tiny field mouse, but she walks across the farm to see Mr. Ages because Timothy needs medicine. Later, she climbs onto Jeremy the crow and flies to the great owl. She is afraid. She goes anyway. 💭 Think: When does YOUR character need courage in your story?

👀 Watch How — Meet Sam, our example writer Meet Sam. Sam is a 4th-grade writer just starting a personal narrative. Today, Sam brainstorms moments from his life and picks ONE that matters. BEFORE Sam’s first list (too big): My summer vacation. Christmas. My birthday. Family camping trip.

📋 Today’s Tool: Memory Brainstorm List 4-6 small moments. Then circle the one with the most FEELING attached. Sam’s brainstorm (filled): 1. The day Bingo got out ← CIRCLED (scariest moment) 2. The time I broke Mom’s favorite cup 3. The first time I rode my bike without help 4. The night the storm took the power out Your turn — brainstorm YOUR moments: List 4 small moments from YOUR life. Then circle the one that still feels alive when you remember it. 1. ______________________ 2. ______________________ 3. ______________________ 4. ______________________

🪶 Sentence Frames You Can Borrow Stuck on how to start? Try one of these: “The time I ___ at ___.” “The day I almost ___.” “The first time I ___.” “The afternoon when ___.” 📝 Now you try. Use what Sam showed you. Borrow a sentence frame if you want. Write below. Pick ONE virtue your story character will live out: courage , honesty , service , perseverance , self-governance , courtesy , or responsibility . Then write one sentence: "My story is about a [character] who shows [virtue] by [doing what]."

Track the tension: Is the problem getting easier or harder to solve? 🧠 As you read this week, watch for: As you read today, watch for how new characters change the direction of the story. What does the owl know about Jonathan Frisby? Why does his name matter so much? 💭 Think about this as you read today — you don't need to write anything here.

📌 Examples rebuild = re- + build (build again) | preheat = pre- + heat (heat before) | unfair = un- + fair (not fair) | dislike = dis- + like (not like) 🧩 Type the missing prefix at the start of each word. un — to take the cover off help — someone who helps rest — taking a break right now kind — in a kind way Check My Work 🌱 All correct!

💎 What is service? Service means helping someone else, especially when they cannot help themselves. 🐭 The book's service moment: Jeremy offers to fly Mrs. Frisby to the owl even though the trip is dangerous at dusk. The owl, who could easily ignore a mouse's problem, listens and gives her real advice — go to the rats. Small acts of service from unexpected helpers keep Mrs. Frisby's hope alive. 💭 Think: How will your character help someone in your story?

👀 Watch How — Meet Sam, our example writer Sam picked his story (the day Bingo got out). Now he maps the SHAPE of his story using the Parts of a Narrative tool. BEFORE Sam’s rough plan: I lost Bingo. I looked for him. I found him.

📋 Today’s Tool: Parts of a Narrative Every personal narrative has 3 parts. Each has its own job. Sam’s narrative map (filled): 🟢 Beginning Set the scene. Hook the reader. I opened the door for the mail. Bingo darted out. 🟡 Middle Events in order. Pressure builds. Called him. Ran in socks. Saw him chasing a squirrel. He almost got hit by a bike. 🔴 End Resolve. Share a feeling or lesson. Caught him. Cried. Learned to close the door.

🪶 Sentence Frames You Can Borrow Stuck on how to start? Try one of these: “It all started when ___.” “Then ___ happened, and ___.” “Just when I thought ___, ___.” “In the end, I learned ___.” 📝 Now you try. Use what Sam showed you. 💎 What is self-governance? keyConcepts: 📌 Examples jumped = jump + -ed (past) | running = run + -ing (now) | taller = tall + -er (more tall) | tallest = tall + -est (most tall) 🎯 Match the word part to its meaning. Tap a part, then tap its meaning. -ed Means 'more' or 'one who does' (taller, faster, helper) -ing Means 'the most' (tallest, fastest, smallest) -er Means 'in the past' (jumped, walked, played) -est Means 'happening now' (running, swimming, jumping)

💎 What is honesty? Honesty means telling the truth, even when it is hard to say. 🐭 The book's honesty moment: Nicodemus could have kept Jonathan's story secret forever. Mrs. Frisby would never have known. He chooses to tell her the truth — about NIMH, about her husband, about how he died. Honesty hurts in that moment. It also frees her. 💭 Think: Where does honesty matter in your story? When does your character tell a hard truth?

👀 Watch How — Meet Sam, our example writer Sam’s draft is done. Today he revises BIG (ARMS) and edits SMALL (CUPS). Both. In that order. BEFORE I run down the street. mom said be careful but I didn't listen. bingo ran into the street. he almost got hit by a bike. I was so scared. I caught him at the park. the end was when I went home.

📋 Today’s Tool: ARMS + CUPS Two checklists. Use ARMS first (big changes). Then CUPS (small fixes). Sam’s ARMS + CUPS work (filled): REVISE: ARMS A dd: dialogue from Mom ✓ R emove: “the end was when” ✓ M ove: heart-pounding detail to ending ✓ S ubstitute: “ran” → “sprinted” ✓ EDIT: CUPS C apitals: M on Mom ✓ U sage: there/their/they’re right? ✓ P unctuation: period after “gone” ✓ S pelling: sprinted (not “sprented”) ✓

Type a new version of your opening sentence.

💎 What is friendship? Friendship is choosing one person to share your life with — your secrets, your imagination, your hopes, your worst days. 🪶 Anne’s moment: Anne has invented Katie Maurice and Violetta because no one stayed. In Ch. 12, she clasps hands with Diana over an imaginary running stream and they vow to be bosom friends forever. It is half-pretend and entirely real. By the end of Ch. 15, when Anne quits school over the slate-and-Gilbert disaster, the deepest grief is leaving Diana. Friendship isn’t the story’s subplot anymore. It is the story. 💭 Think: Who is the most important person in YOUR character’s life? How will their friendship show up in your story?

👀 Watch How — Meet Sam, our example writer Sam now knows his story will have a problem. Today, Sam maps the parts of his story using the Parts of a Narrative tool: strong beginning, strong middle, strong ending. BEFORE Sam’s rough plan: Mateo goes to tryouts. He’s scared. He makes the team.

📋 Today’s Tool: Parts of a Narrative A strong narrative has three parts. Each part has its own job. Sam’s narrative map (filled): 🟢 Beginning Hook the reader. Introduce character + setting. Mateo wants to make the team but is scared. 🟡 Middle Tell events in order. Use transitions. Show feelings. Diego signs up. Mateo almost quits twice. He trips during sprints. 🔴 End Rephrase opening. Tell feelings. Share a lesson. Mateo gets up and finishes — before he even sees the list.

🪶 Sentence Frames You Can Borrow Stuck on how to start? Try one of these: “[Character] wanted ___ more than anything.” “But ___ kept getting in the way.” “Just when [character] thought ___, ___ happened.” “In the end, [character] ___.” 📝 Now you try. Use what Sam showed you. Borrow a sentence frame if you want. Write below. Conflict starts with desire. Write 2-3 sentences: name ONE specific thing your character wants (a thing, a friend, a place, a moment). Then name ONE thing or person that makes it hard to get.

💎 What is courage? Courage is not the absence of fear. It is doing the hard thing while you are still afraid. 🪶 Anne’s moment: In Ch. 18, Anne runs through the dark and snow to save Diana’s baby sister from croup. Young Mary Joe is frozen. Diana is crying. Anne — the orphan girl whose past everyone calls hard — is the only one who knows what to do, because she helped raise three sets of twins. Her hard past becomes her gift. The doctor says she saved the baby’s life. Anne’s courage isn’t loud. It is what she does when she has training and everyone else has fear. 💭 Think: When does YOUR character have to do the hard thing while still being scared? What gives them the courage to act?

👀 Watch How — Meet Sam, our example writer Sam is drafting his opening. He tries different Beginning Leads to see which one hooks the reader best. BEFORE It was a sunny day. Mateo woke up. He was nervous about soccer tryouts.

📋 Today’s Tool: Beginning Leads Six ways to hook your reader. Pick ONE for your story. Sam’s six possible openings (he picks #2): 1. Question Have you ever wanted something so bad you almost didn’t try? 2. Dialogue ✓ (Sam picks this) “You’re going to be late!” Mom shouted. 3. Action I tied my cleat. I untied it. I tied it again. 4. Sound effect RIIIIIIING. The phone. Then Mom screamed my name. 5. Snapshot The cleats sat by the door, untouched. 6. Flashback I had wanted to make this team since I was seven.

🪶 Sentence Frames You Can Borrow Stuck on how to start? Try one of these: “Have you ever ___?” (Question lead) “‘___,’ [someone] [verb]-ed.” (Dialogue lead) “[Character] [vivid verb]-ed the ___.” (Action lead) “The ___ sat ___, untouched.” (Snapshot lead) 📝 Now you try. Use what Sam showed you. Borrow a sentence frame if you want. Write below. Draft your story’s opening. Write 3-5 sentences. Open with your character DOING something specific. No feelings yet, no weather. Just action. Use present-tense verbs if you want it to feel immediate.

💎 What is being seen? Being seen is having someone notice who you really are — not just what you look like or what you do, but what matters to you, what you long for, what makes you, you. 🪶 Anne’s moment: In Ch. 25, Matthew — the shyest man in Avonlea — walks into a strange store and tries to buy Anne a dress. He is so flustered by the lady clerk that he buys a garden rake and 20 pounds of brown sugar by mistake. Then he asks Mrs. Lynde for help. On Christmas morning, Anne unwraps a soft brown dress with the puffed sleeves she has longed for since Ch. 11. Matthew, who barely speaks, has been watching Anne all year. He saw what she wanted most. He saw it, and he did the bravest thing he could to give it to her. 💭 Think: Who in YOUR character’s life truly sees them? What small thing could that person do that would change everything?

👀 Watch How — Meet Sam, our example writer Sam writes the middle of his story. He uses the Stoplight Writing organizer to plot events in order — and Transition words to glue them together. BEFORE Mateo tried out. He was nervous. He did the drills. He waited.

keyConcepts: 📌 Examples transport = trans- + port (to carry across) | portable = port + able (able to be carried) | attract = at- + tract (to draw toward) | distract = dis- + tract (to draw apart) 🧩 Type the missing prefix at the start of each word. trans — to carry across (a truck transports goods) ex — to carry out (sell to another country) at — to draw toward; pull in dis — to draw apart (lose focus) Check My Work 🌱 All correct!
📌 Let’s try it together: “diligent”

Group A — drop the silent e before a vowel suffix save → sav ing · like → lik ed · hope → hop ing Group B — KEEP the e after ce/ge before a/o suffix courag e + ous = courag e ous · notic e + able = notic e able

💎 What is learning from mistakes? Growing up doesn’t mean not making mistakes. It means looking at each mistake honestly and letting it teach you something specific. 🪶 Anne’s moment: After Anne falls off the leaking flat playing Elaine, she tells Marilla: “The brooch cured me of meddling. The Haunted Wood cured me of letting my imagination run away. The liniment cake cured me of carelessness in cooking. Dyeing my hair cured me of vanity. And today’s mistake is going to cure me of being too romantic.” Anne is growing up not because she stops making mistakes — she is growing up because she can now NAME what each one has taught her. 💭 Think: What is one mistake your character could make in your story — and what could it teach them?

👀 Watch How — Meet Sam, our example writer Sam’s draft is on the page. Now he revises with ARMS. Each letter is a different kind of change. BEFORE Mateo tried out. He did some drills. The drills were hard. Mateo was sad. He kicked the ball. Mateo’s dad came to watch. The end of the day was good. Mateo went home. He was tired. He talked to his mom. Then he went to bed.

📋 Today’s Tool: ARMS (Revising Checklist) Think ARMS as you revise. Each letter is a different move. Sam’s ARMS checklist (filled): A dd ➕ Sensory detail in the tryout scene: “sweat ran down his neck” ✓ R emove ➖ The sentence about Mateo’s dad arriving (it interrupts the scene) ✓ M ove ↔ Diego helping Mateo up — move it earlier in the scene ✓ S ubstitute 🔄 Boring word “kicked” → specific word “slammed” ✓

🪶 Sentence Frames You Can Borrow Stuck on how to start? Try one of these: “I will ADD a sensory detail when ___.” “I will REMOVE the part where ___.” “I will MOVE ___ to ___.” “I will SUBSTITUTE ___ for ___.” 📝 Now you try. Use what Sam showed you. Borrow a sentence frame if you want. Write below. Pacing pass. Re-read your draft. Find ONE place that moves too fast (jumped over something the reader needs). Write 2-3 sentences to ADD there. Then find ONE place that moves too slow. Mark what you would cut.

💎 What is knowing who you are? Knowing who you are means understanding what stays the same about you even when everything around you changes. 🪶 Anne’s moment: In Ch. 34, on the night before Anne leaves for Queen’s, Marilla cries because the girl she loves is going away. Anne sits down on Marilla’s lap, takes her face in both hands, and says: “I’m not a bit changed — not really. I’m only just pruned down and branched out. The real me — back here — is just the same.” Anne has grown two inches. She is quieter. She uses smaller words. She is leaving for the city. But the part of her that loves Marilla and Matthew and Green Gables — that part is still right there. Knowing that is what makes her ready to go. 💭 Think: What stays the same about YOUR character no matter what happens? What is the heart of them?

💎 What is the bend in the road? Growing up means you can’t always see what’s coming. Sometimes the road turns. The hardest part of growing up — and the bravest — is choosing love over what you thought you wanted. 🪶 Anne’s moment: In Ch. 38, Anne tells Marilla she will not go to Redmond. She will stay home, teach at Carmody, and care for Marilla’s failing eyes. Then Gilbert — the boy she called ‘Carrots’ in Ch. 15 and refused to forgive for years — gives up the Avonlea school so Anne can teach close to home. They stand at the gate for half an hour. They are friends now. Anne looks down the road she didn’t plan for and says: ‘I don’t know what lies around the bend, but I’m going to believe that the best does.’ That is the heart of the whole novel. Anne started as the orphan at the train station who nobody wanted. She ends as a young woman choosing the life she has — on purpose. 💭 Think: What is a ‘bend in the road’ YOUR character might face? How will they choose to meet it?

📋 Today’s Tool: Strong Endings A strong ending can do one of these moves (pick one): Sam’s plan for his ending: Rephrase your beginning Start: “The field looked huge.” End: “The field felt small.” Tell your feelings “Mateo felt steady for the first time all day.” Share a lesson learned “Being scared and trying anyway is what brave is.” Share a hope for the future “Next year I won’t be scared at all.”

💎 What is the bend in the road? Growing up means you can’t always see what’s coming. Sometimes the road turns. The hardest part of growing up — and the bravest — is choosing love over what you thought you wanted. 🪶 Anne’s moment: In Ch. 38, Anne tells Marilla she will not go to Redmond. She will stay home, teach at Carmody, and care for Marilla’s failing eyes. Then Gilbert — the boy she called ‘Carrots’ in Ch. 15 and refused to forgive for years — gives up the Avonlea school so Anne can teach close to home. They stand at the gate for half an hour. 💎 The Q3 lens Last quarter we watched Anne grow up. This quarter, we watch people show COURAGE — and we get ready to read a novel where ordinary people did extraordinary things to save their neighbors. 🛡️ What is courage? Courage is not the absence of fear. Courage is being scared AND doing the right thing anyway. 📖 This week’s moment: Even reading about hard history takes courage. Today, we’re learning facts about a frightening time — WWII, the Nazis, the Holocaust. It’s OK to feel uncomfortable. Real courage is staying with the truth even when it’s hard. 💭 Think: When have YOU been brave when you were also scared? Name one small moment.

📜 Source Passage World War II began in 1939, when the country of Germany attacked Poland. Germany was led by a man named Adolf Hitler. Hitler led a political group called the Nazis. He had taken power in Germany in 1933 and built up a huge army. Hitler wanted Germany to rule over more land. He invaded one country after another — Austria, Czechoslovakia, Poland, France, the Netherlands, Norway, and many more. By 1941, Germany had conquered most of Europe. Britain, France, and later the United States and the Soviet Union fought against Germany. They were called the Allies. The war finally ended in 1945, when the Allies defeated Germany. Six years of fighting had changed the world. Adapted from U.S. Holocaust Memorial Museum & standard history ⏸️ Pause After Passage 1 Most of Europe was under Nazi rule by 1941. What does that tell you about how powerful Germany was at that point? 💭 Pause and think about this — no need to write.

💎 The Q3 lens King Christian X of Denmark didn’t fight the Germans with weapons. He stood on his throne and refused to act ashamed of his country’s Jewish citizens. 🛡️ What is courage? Courage isn’t always loud. Sometimes courage is REFUSING to do what a bully tells you — staying on your principles even when staying costs you. 📖 This week’s moment: The famous (untrue) story that King Christian X said he would wear a yellow star himself shows what the Danish people believed about courage: that a leader stands with his people, not above them. 💭 Think: Have you ever stood up for someone who was being treated unfairly? 📜 Source Passage Germany invaded Denmark on April 9, 1940. Within a few hours, Denmark had surrendered. The Danish king, Christian X, stayed on his throne. Denmark’s government kept running the country’s daily life — schools, police, hospitals. At first, German soldiers in Denmark acted differently than in other countries. They did not make Jewish people register their names or wear special yellow badges. The German leaders wanted to keep the Danes calm so that food and supplies would keep flowing to Germany. But everyone knew the truth: Germany was in charge. Danish people who spoke against the Nazis could be arrested. By 1943, secret groups of brave Danes had started a Resistance — people who pushed back against the German rules in quiet, careful ways. 💎 The Q3 lens It wasn’t just kings or soldiers who showed courage. It was teachers, fishermen, doctors, schoolchildren. People who hid families in basements. People who pretended to be sick. People who looked the other way at the right moment. 🛡️ What is courage? Most courage is small. Quiet. Made of a thousand small choices — not one big speech. 📖 This week’s moment: A Danish doctor wrote down fake names on hospital records so the Nazis couldn’t find Jewish patients. A fisherman lent his boat without asking for money. A neighbor kept a child safe for one week, then handed her to another neighbor for the next week. Each act was small. Together they saved 7,200 lives. 💭 Think: What is a small courageous choice you could make this week — even one nobody else would notice?

📜 Source Passage In many countries under Nazi rule, Jewish people were forced to wear a six-pointed yellow star sewn onto their clothes. It was called the Star of David. The Nazis used this badge to mark Jewish people as different — and as targets. Jewish people in countries like Poland, France, Belgium, and the Netherlands had to wear the star every day. They could be arrested for not wearing it. Many were taken from their homes and sent to concentration camps. Denmark was different. The Danish government refused to require Jewish people to wear the star. The Danish king and many Danish people stood by their Jewish neighbors. A famous story says that King Christian X himself promised to wear a yellow star if the Nazis tried to force the law. The story isn’t exactly true, but it shows what Danes believed about their king — and about themselves. Adapted from the U.S. Holocaust Memorial Museum ⏸️ Pause After Passage 3 Most countries forced Jewish people to wear the yellow star. Denmark refused. keyConcepts: 📌 Examples connect = con- + nect (join together) | combine = com- + bine (mix together) | company = com- + pany (those who go together) | conversation = con- + verse (turning words together) 🧩 Type the missing prefix at the start of each word. nect — to join together bine — to mix together pany — people together tinue — to keep going (with what you started) Check My Work 🌱 All correct!
📌 Let's try it together: "companion"
Group A — just add -s cat → cat s · road → road s · book → book s · tree → tree s Group B — add -es OR change y to i + es box → box es · brush → brush es · puppy → pupp ies · story → stor ies

💎 The Q3 lens Almost everyone in Denmark’s rescue story has died. The fishermen, the families they saved, the king. Lois Lowry wrote Number the Stars so we would remember them. 🛡️ What is courage? One kind of courage is remembering — not forgetting the people who did the brave thing, and not forgetting the people who got hurt. 📖 This week’s moment: This quarter, you will read about a 10-year-old girl named Annemarie who shows courage in the middle of all this. By learning her story, you join the people who remember. 💭 Think: Who in your life has done something brave that should be remembered? Could you write about them someday?

📜 Source Passage By the fall of 1943, the Nazis decided to deport Denmark’s Jewish people — about 7,500 men, women, and children — to concentration camps. The plan was set for October 1, 1943. But a brave German man named Georg Duckwitz secretly warned Danish leaders before the roundup began. Word spread through churches, schools, and small Danish towns within hours. Jewish families left their homes and hid — in churches, in basements, in farmhouses, in hospitals. Doctors registered Jewish people as fake patients. Fishermen offered their boats. Police looked the other way. Over the next few weeks, Danish people smuggled more than 7,200 Jewish people and 700 of their non-Jewish family members across the cold sea to Sweden — a country that took them in. Most of them survived the war. Only about 120 Danish Jews died in the Holocaust. That is one of the highest survival rates of any country in Nazi-occupied Europe. Lois Lowry wrote a novel called Number the Stars about a girl who lived through this rescue. It is the book we will read this quarter. Adapted from the U.S. Holocaust Memorial Museum ⏸️ Pause After Passage 4 More than 7,200 Jewish people were saved in one month. What had to be true about the Danish people for this to happen? 💭 Pause and think about this — no need to write.

👀 Watch How — Meet Sam, our example writer Meet Sam. Sam is a 4th-grade writer just starting a realistic-fiction story about Mateo Hernandez, a kid who’s scared to try out for the soccer team. Today, Sam works on Mateo’s VOICE — choosing specific words. BEFORE Mateo was nervous. He looked at the field. He felt bad.

📋 Today’s Tool: Specific Words Great writing has words that are specific, vivid, and descriptive . Sam’s word-choice planner (filled): Type Boring Specific / Vivid Adjective nice field green, freshly cut field Vivid verb said quietly whispered Vivid verb went fast sprinted, raced, dashed Specific noun a boy Mateo

🪶 Sentence Frames You Can Borrow Stuck on how to start? Try one of these: “[Character]’s [body part] felt ___.” “[Character] [vivid verb]-ed ___.” “‘___,’ [character] whispered/shouted/mumbled.” “The ___ was [specific adjective].” 📝 Now you try. Use what Sam showed you. Borrow a sentence frame if you want. Write below. Week 7 brainstorm: Pick a growing-up aspect your character will face (imagination, friendship, mistakes, ambition, etc.). Then write one sentence: "My story is about a [character] who [realistic situation] and learns about [aspect]."

💎 The Q3 lens Courage doesn’t always look brave. Sometimes it looks like a 10-year-old answering a soldier’s question without crying. 🛡️ What is courage today? Sometimes courage is being scared and choosing your words carefully anyway. It’s slowing down when your heart is racing. 📖 This chapter’s moment: When the soldier asks Annemarie why she was running, she answers carefully. She doesn’t lie, exactly. She doesn’t panic. That is the first quiet act of courage in the book. 💭 Think: When have you had to stay calm and pick your words even though you were nervous?

👀 Watch How — Sam, our example writer Sam is starting his Q3 opinion essay. He has to pick a character moment from Number the Stars Ch. 1 that shows courage or loyalty — something he can argue about. BEFORE Sam’s vague idea: ‘Annemarie is brave.’

📋 Today’s Tool: Moment Picker Find ONE moment in Ch. 1 where a character shows courage or loyalty. Two questions to check it. Sam’s picked moment (filled): Moment: When the German soldier stops Annemarie, she stays calm and answers him carefully even though she’s scared. Does it show COURAGE or LOYALTY? Courage — she chose her words carefully when she was afraid. Can I find evidence in the chapter? Yes — the way she answers without crying or running, and what Mama says afterward.

📝 Your Essay Draft So Far Your opinion essay grows across the whole unit. Each day you add a piece. 💎 The Q3 lens A padlocked button shop is easy to walk past. Annemarie doesn’t. She asks. She wants to know. 🛡️ What is courage today? One kind of courage is paying attention — refusing to look away when something has changed for the worse. 📖 This chapter’s moment: Annemarie sees that Mrs. Hirsch’s shop is closed. She asks Papa about it. She doesn’t pretend nothing happened. That noticing is brave. 💭 Think: Have you ever noticed something unfair, even when no one else said anything? What did you do?
👀 Watch How — Sam, our example writer Sam has his claim about Annemarie’s courage. Today he adds three SPECIFIC reasons that support it. BEFORE Sam’s one big reason: She didn’t run.

📌 Why Writers Use Them Without prepositional phrases, writing is flat: “Harriet moved.” With prepositional phrases, writing comes alive: “Harriet moved through the night , across the frozen river , with a lantern in her hand .” Sterling stacks prepositional phrases to put readers inside Harriet’s world — you feel where she is, when it happens, and how she moves. 🎮 Prepositional phrase spotter: In each sentence, tap the first word of the prepositional phrase. Harriet led her people through the darkest nights.

👁 The 3-Move Conclusion Move 1: Restate — Say your main idea again in different words. Do NOT copy your introduction. Move 2: Summarize — Point back to your strongest pieces of evidence. One or two sentences: “From ___ to ___, the evidence shows that…” Move 3: Lasting Thought — End with something worth thinking about. Why does this still matter? What does the reader carry away? 📌 Sentence Frames to Help You Start Move 1: “Throughout her life, Harriet Tubman showed that…” | “The evidence in this essay reveals that…” Move 2: “From ___ to ___, we see that…” | “Whether she was ___ or ___, Harriet always…” Move 3: “Today, Harriet’s story reminds us that…” | “The freedom she carried was not just her own —” Write your 3-move conclusion. Aim for 4–6 sentences. Label the three moves if it helps you check your work.

keyConcepts: 📌 Why Commas in a Series Matter Without commas: “The soldiers destroyed cotton commissary stores and dwellings.” — Wait, is “cotton commissary stores” one thing or two? It’s confusing! With commas: “The soldiers destroyed cotton, commissary stores, and dwellings.” — Now we see three separate items clearly. Look at Source A from this week: the Wisconsin State Journal writer listed what was destroyed using commas in a series. Without those commas, the sentence would be a jumble. 🤔 Think about it: Read this sentence without commas and think about what could go wrong: “Harriet carried a lantern a pistol and medicine.” Is “a lantern a pistol” one item? Add the commas in your mind to see the three separate items.

📌 Presentation Tips Read clearly: Slow down. Let your audience follow your ideas. Use expression: Your voice should match the importance of what you’re saying. Look up: If you can, make eye contact with your audience between sentences. After practicing your presentation, answer: What is your essay about? What is ONE thing you want your audience to remember? Write 2–3 sentences summarizing your essay and your key finding.

keyConcepts: 📌 Three Bases to Know This Week rupt = break | duct / duce = lead | form = shape interrupt = to break in on • conduct = to lead or direct • transform = to change shape or form completely More examples — rupt: erupt, rupture, disrupt, abrupt, corrupt duct/duce: produce, introduce, deduce, reduce, aqueduct form: reform, uniform, conform, inform, formulate Use the word bases to fill in the blanks. Tap the correct word for each sentence. “Aslan’s roar seemed to _______ the silence of the forest all at once.” disrupt conduct reform

📌 Three-Step Decode: precipice Step 1 — Context: “They were on the edge of a precipice .” What clues does the sentence give you? Edge suggests something steep or dangerous. Step 2 — Word Parts: precipice comes from Latin praeceps — prae (before) + caput (head). Think: “headfirst” — a place so steep you’d fall head-first. Step 3 — Confirm: precipice = a very steep cliff face; a dangerous drop-off edge. Now try the remaining three words. Think first — what might each word mean? Then tap to flip and check. 🔍 bivouac Tap to flip

📌 Two Rules to Know Dates: When you write a full date, put a comma between the day number and the year. Example: The children returned to Narnia on June 4 , 1941. Places: When you write a city and state (or city and country), put a comma between them. Example: Lucy grew up in London , England before she went to Narnia. Read these example sentences. Notice where the commas appear and why. The Pevensies arrived in Narnia on August 10 , and Lucy was the first one to see Aslan. The comma separates the date element from the rest of the sentence. Professor Kirke lived in Oxford , England , and his house held a very unusual wardrobe. A comma separates city from country. Another comma comes after the country when the sentence continues. 💭 The pattern: Commas in dates and places signal a pause — they separate one piece of location or time information from the next. Think of it as a way of organizing information so the reader doesn’t get confused. Tomorrow you’ll practice identifying where commas belong in date and place sentences on your own. For today, just study these examples and notice the pattern.

📌 Three-Step Decode: solemnly (from Number the Stars ) Step 1 — Context: Annemarie nodded solemnly and promised she would be brave. What clues does the sentence give you? “Nodded” and “promised” suggest this is a very serious moment. Step 2 — Word Parts: solemn (serious, grave) + -ly (adverb suffix meaning “in that way”). So solemnly means “in a serious, grave way.” Step 3 — Confirm: solemnly = done or said in a very serious, sincere way. Now try the remaining words. Think first — what might each mean? 📌 Major Spelling Patterns from This Year Doubling rule: Double the final consonant before adding -ing or -ed to a short-vowel word ending in one consonant. ( run → running ) Drop-e rule: Drop the silent e before a vowel suffix. ( write → writing ) Change-y rule: Change y to i before adding -es or -ed (unless the y follows a vowel). ( carry → carried ) au / aw: Both make the same /ô/ sound. au usually appears in the middle of a word; aw often comes at the end. ( caught, draw ) ei / ie: Use ie after most letters; use ei after c or when the sound is /ā/. ( believe, receive, eight ) Sort these 8 words by their spelling pattern. info.detail: Anne · Number the Stars · Prince Caspian
info.label: Reading

keyConcepts: 📌 All-Year Root Reference rupt = break | port = carry | scrib/script = write | spec/spect = look/watch | domin = master/rule | reg/rupt = rule/break Examples: erupt, transport, inscription, spectator, dominate, regulate Match each word to the meaning of its root. Tap a word, then tap its meaning. erupt transport inscription spectator dominate regulate break out carry across something written one who looks or watches to master or control to rule or make right

📌 What These Words Mean indignant (Anne) — feeling angry or annoyed because something is unfair. Anne felt indignant when Mrs. Lynde criticized her hair. vexed (Anne) — troubled or irritated. Marilla was vexed when Anne forgot her chores. solemnly (NTS) — in a serious, formal, or deeply sincere way. Annemarie solemnly promised to be brave. occupation (NTS) — the control of a country by a military force of another nation. During the German occupation, the Jews of Denmark were in danger. allegiance (PC) — loyalty or commitment to a leader, country, or cause. The Old Narnians swore allegiance to Prince Caspian. sovereign (PC) — a supreme ruler; having complete power. Aslan was the sovereign over all of Narnia.

📌 Grammar Rules We’ve Studied Proper noun capitalization — names of people, places, and specific titles are always capitalized. Comma in dialogue — a comma separates the speaker tag from the spoken words. Quotation marks — go around the exact words someone speaks. keyConcepts: 📌 Your Year of Word Roots — Cumulative Reference Card struct = build — construct, structure rupt = break — disrupt, erupt port = carry — transport, import tract = pull — distract, attract scrib/script = write — inscribe, describe duct = lead — conduct, introduce form = shape — transform, uniform spec/spect = look — inspect, spectator reg/rect = rule/straight — correct, region domin = master — dominant, dominion voc/vok = voice/call — vocal, provoke ject = throw — reject, subject

📌 Three-Step Decode: solemnly (from Number the Stars ) Step 1 — Context: Annemarie nodded solemnly and promised she would be brave. What clues does the sentence give you? “Nodded” and “promised” suggest this is a very serious moment. Step 2 — Word Parts: solemn (serious, grave) + -ly (adverb suffix meaning “in that way”). So solemnly means “in a serious, grave way.” Step 3 — Confirm: solemnly = done or said in a very serious, sincere way. Now try the remaining words. Think first — what might each mean? Then tap to flip and check. ⚔️ allegiance Prince Caspian Tap to flip

📌 Major Spelling Patterns from This Year Doubling rule: Double the final consonant before adding -ing or -ed to a short-vowel word ending in one consonant. ( run → running ) Drop-e rule: Drop the silent e before a vowel suffix. ( write → writing ) Change-y rule: Change y to i before adding -es or -ed (unless the y follows a vowel). ( carry → carried ) au / aw: Both make the same /ô/ sound. au usually appears in the middle of a word; aw often comes at the end. ( caught, draw ) ei / ie: Use ie after most letters; use ei after c or when the sound is /ā/. ( believe, receive, eight ) Sort these 8 words by their spelling pattern. Tap a word from the bank, then tap the correct column. running writing carried caught draw believe receive racing Doubling

📌 What Makes a Strong Comparison Paragraph? Opening sentence: Names both novels and hints at the shared theme — not just “Both books have themes.” Evidence from each novel: A specific moment, character action, or quote — not a vague summary. Connection: A sentence that explains HOW the two examples connect to the same theme. Closing sentence: Returns to the big idea and leaves the reader thinking. Mark at least two places in your paragraph where you can improve. Then use those marks when you write your revised paragraph in the Assignment tab.

📌 What These Words Mean indignant (Anne) — feeling angry or annoyed because something is unfair. Anne felt indignant when Mrs. Lynde criticized her hair. vexed (Anne) — troubled or irritated. Marilla was vexed when Anne forgot her chores. solemnly (NTS) — in a serious, formal, or deeply sincere way. Annemarie solemnly promised to be brave. occupation (NTS) — the control of a country by a military force of another nation. During the German occupation, the Jews of Denmark were in danger. allegiance (PC) — loyalty or commitment to a leader, country, or cause. The Old Narnians swore allegiance to Prince Caspian. sovereign (PC) — a supreme ruler; having complete power. Aslan was the sovereign over all of Narnia.

📌 Grammar Rules We’ve Studied Proper noun capitalization — names of people, places, and specific titles are always capitalized. Comma in dialogue — a comma separates the speaker tag from the spoken words. Quotation marks — go around the exact words someone speaks. Course Overview

Grade 4 Language Arts develops close reading, literary and informational analysis, vocabulary, morphology, grammar, fluent oral reading, research, speaking, and written expression. Students use evidence to explain character, perspective, theme, central idea, author choices, and relationships across texts.

Core Course Areas
• Literature, historical fiction, biography, and informational text
• What Good Readers Do
• RWM and author’s craft
• Greek and Latin roots, affixes, bases, and word origins
• Spelling and multisyllabic word analysis
• Grammar and conventions
• Weekly fluency practice
• Narrative, realistic fiction, opinion, research, and literary analysis
• Speaking, presentation, and multimedia work
• Portfolio and final cross-text synthesis
A Typical ELA Learning Pathway
Welcome and Roadmap Learn the objective, reading assignment, materials, and order of work.
Language and Word Study Practice morphology, vocabulary, spelling, grammar, or sentence analysis.
Reading Focus Read with a Good Reader lens and track meaningful evidence.
Teacher Modeling Study examples of close reading, analysis, fluency, or writing decisions.
Application and Writing Use reading, vocabulary, grammar, and craft knowledge in a response or project.
Self-Check and Turn-In Review evidence, revise, edit, and submit the required work.
How Work Is Reviewed
Area What Strong Work Shows
Reading and Analysis The response accurately explains the text, its structure, and important relationships.
Evidence Claims and explanations are supported with relevant details or quotations when assigned.
Writing and Organization The writing fits its purpose, develops ideas, and uses clear structure and transitions.
Language and Craft Vocabulary, sentence variety, grammar, punctuation, spelling, and author’s craft support meaning.
Revision and Communication The student revises thoughtfully and communicates clearly in written, spoken, or multimedia form.
Fluency, Writing, and Spotlight Tasks

Fluency: Most weeks include listening to a model, practicing accuracy and smoothness, reading with expression, and submitting a final recording.

Writing projects: Students complete guided narrative, realistic fiction, opinion, research, and literary-analysis work through planning, drafting, revising, editing, publishing, and reflection.

Spotlight Tasks: Weekly Spotlight Task pages provide an additional reading, speaking, writing, discussion, or immersive activity connected to the week’s text and skills.

You will analyze characters and themes, build vocabulary through Greek and Latin roots, strengthen grammar and fluency, and write narratives, opinions, research pieces, and literary responses.

Books and Course Modules
Each section contains its assigned weeks, daily reading lessons, weekly fluency work, Spotlight Tasks, and writing activities.
1 Mrs. Frisby and the Rats of NIMH Weeks 1–6 Character, conflict, motivation, prediction, theme, narrative writing, morphology review, and fluency 2 Anne of Green Gables Weeks 7–14 Point of view, character growth, setting, summary, theme, realistic fiction, Greek and Latin roots, and fluency
3 Number the Stars Weeks 15–19 Historical context, inference, courage, symbolism, fiction and nonfiction comparison, opinion writing, and fluency 4 Freedom Train Weeks 20–25 Biography, central idea, chronology, cause and effect, author perspective, research writing, sources, and presentation
5 Prince Caspian Weeks 26–30 Fantasy setting, multiple character groups, leadership, conflict, theme, literary analysis, and fluency 6 Year-End Synthesis & Portfolio Weeks 31–32 Cross-text comparison, reading growth, grammar and morphology review, final presentation, portfolio, and reflection
Reader and Writer Spotlight
Strong readers notice patterns across a whole text.

Track repeated choices, images, conflicts, and ideas. Those patterns often help reveal character growth, perspective, and theme.

New Here? Start Here
Everything you need before beginning Grade 4 Language Arts.
GRADE 4 ELA
Welcome, Reader and Writer!

Your ELA course is a guided learning pathway. Teacher videos, reading frames, sentence study, morphology, language practice, writing checkpoints, self-checks, and turn-in directions will guide you through each week.

How Each Week Is Organized
1
Open the assigned week
Begin with the first unfinished daily lesson.
2
Read with a purpose
Use the Good Reader focus while reading the assigned chapters or text.
3
Analyze and apply
Practice morphology, grammar, vocabulary, RWM, and writing.
4
Review and submit
Revise carefully and submit the required written or recorded response.
Course Routines You Will See
What Good Readers Do A focused habit for noticing character, perspective, conflict, theme, structure, or evidence.
RWM Read like a Reader, Read like a Writer, and Mimic an author’s sentence pattern or craft choice.
Morphology Use Greek and Latin roots, prefixes, suffixes, bases, and word origins to unlock meaning.
Fluency Listen, practice accuracy and smoothness, read with expression, then record the final reading.
Writing Workshop Plan, draft, revise, edit, publish, and reflect on a larger piece of writing.
Before You Begin

Make sure you can find your assigned books or readings, Modules, weekly lessons, Spotlight Tasks, the Course Guide, and your teacher’s contact information.
